claims.text: Unmodified CoCrFeNi has difficulty maintaining low friction and wear across room temperature to 800 °C.
An ultrathin, nanostructured gradient tribo-coating will provide adaptive tribological protection to CoCrFeNi.
The coating will consistently reduce the coefficient of friction from 25 °C to 800 °C relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
The coating will consistently reduce the specific wear rate from 25 °C to 800 °C relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
The tribological improvements will persist under loads ranging from low to high.
The intervention will remain effective in both ambient air and inert atmospheres.
At low temperature, the gradient tribo-layer will maintain metallic bonding.
At low temperature, the gradient tribo-layer will provide low shear resistance.
The low-shear coating interface will diminish adhesive wear at lower temperatures.
At high temperature, controlled tribo-oxidation of the gradient coating will form a stable, lubricious nanocrystalline glaze layer.
The nanocrystalline glaze layer will minimize adhesive and oxidative wear by acting as a protective barrier.
The gradient structure will adapt to or release friction-induced strain or stress gradients.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has higher friction and wear because its surface characteristics fail to adapt over the full temperature range.
Rapid temperature changes may prevent sufficiently fast formation of the protective glaze.
Extreme loads outside the typical testing range may limit coating performance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant and consistent reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the specified test matrix will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the proposed adaptive lubricious glaze layer will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: High-temperature protection is attributed to controlled oxidation and glaze formation, yet effectiveness is also claimed in inert atmospheres, where oxidation may be suppressed. No alternative high-temperature inert-atmosphere mechanism is specified, while absence of the glaze is itself defined as falsifying.

The hypothesis and boundary claim effectiveness under varying conditions including both oxidizing and inert environments, whereas the predicted outcome explicitly promises performance under variable loads and oxidizing environments but does not clearly make the corresponding inert-environment prediction.
